Lab 032 · Lesson 032 · simulation using the lesson's numbers

Tile Lab

The harbor frame on a tile-based phone GPU. Each render pass draws on the chip; only its loads and stores go to main memory. Change them and watch the frame's bytes, not only its milliseconds.

Lantern Harbor at sunset, mid-range phone, MSAA 4×. Goal: ≤ 180 MB per frame (about 5.3 GB/s at 30 fps) so the phone stays cool, and GPU ≤ 28 ms.

Lesson 032: tile-based rendering and bandwidth

    
    
  
    

  
    
    
    What this shows
    
    
    
      
    The chip is cheap, the walk is not
    Depth tests, blending and MSAA samples happen in tile memory. Only loads and stores reach main memory: 4.39 MB per buffer, 17.58 MB with MSAA 4×.
    
      
    Pass breaks multiply trips
    The water's screen copies split one pass into three. The same screen went to memory and back again and again: 114 MB per frame.
    
      
    Bytes are heat
    From 307 to 172 MB per frame, GPU time stays at 19 ms. Bandwidth falls by 44%, and that is the difference between a hot phone and a cool one.
    
    
    
    
    This lab is a simulation, not a measurement. It uses the lesson's numbers: one 1600 × 720 × 4-byte buffer is 4.39 MB, textures and vertex data are 140 MB, post is 24 MB, memory work is about 20 MB per ms, the pixel station is 16 ms, and the team's budget of 180 MB per frame comes from its long-play tests. Real phones also compress buffers (AFBC, UBWC), which lowers the real bytes, and heat depends on much more than memory traffic.
